answer_1.quote: This paper aims to bridge this gap. Firstly, to address the data scarcity issue, we propose a method for generating high-quality synthetic CSW GEC data, using which we produce, to our knowledge, one of the first substantial datasets labelled for this task. Secondly, we train a token classification-style GEC system, tailored to correct errors in texts produced by ESL learners.
answer_1.outputs: Grammatically corrected text and synthetic code-switched text

answer_2.quote: The ER-RANT GEC evaluation results, as outlined in Table , demonstrate a clear degradation in performance when these two systems are applied to CSW texts. The ERRANT toolkit detects and classifies edits between source and target sentence pairs into predefined error categories. It enables the comparison of a proposed set of edits with a reference set, providing a way of calculating metrics, such as precision and recall, across these categories. ... We used several CSW metrics to quantify the qualities of CSW texts: Code Mixing Index (CMI) (Gambäck and Das, 2016), Multilingual Index (M-Index), Probability of Switching (I-Index), Burstiness, and Complexity Factor (CF1-3).
